newsitem.title: RUSSIA: German gets Russian spacecraft commander's licence.
newsitem.headline: German gets Russian spacecraft commander's licence.

text.p: German Thomas Reiter on Thursday became the first foreigner authorised to command the Russian-made Soyuz spaceships which carry crews to and from the space station Mir.

"I am very satisfied," Reiter, 38, told reporters with a smile after getting out of a Soyuz model during the final stage of his training programmme in the Zvyozdny Gorodok Cosmonauts Training Centre outside Moscow.

"The Soyuz capsule has a very high level of automatic control...But manoeuvres with manual controls are also very important, and that is what we just did," he said, lifting one of his helmet's ear pads to hear questions better.
A European Space Agency official said he expected Reiter, a pilot from Frankfurt, to put his skills to use when the international space station Alpha replaces Mir in the next few years.

"Reiter succeeded in commanding Soyuz. He has the qualification. I keep my fingers crossed hoping that some time in future he will lead German crews to the international station Alpha," said the official.
"He did a good job and he is very motivated," he added.
The development of the multi-billion-dollar, permanently-manned orbiting space station Alpha is funded jointly by Russia, the United States, Europe, Canada and Japan.
Soyuz capsules will be used in the Alpha project as one of the means to transport crews and as lifeboats.
Last year Reiter spent almost six weightless months on Russia's Mir space station with two Russian crew-mates, Sergei Avdayev and Yuri Gidzenko.
The flight included a cliff-hanger moment in November when they had to repair a leaking cooling pipe. Reiter also performed two complicated spacewalks, installing scientific equipment outside Mir.
Since then, Mir has suffered a number of mishaps, including a fire and a collision with an unmanned freighter during a training manoeuvre, the worst accident in its 11-year history.
Reiter said he expected the two Russian cosmonauts heading to Mir in August to fix all problems at the station which had originally been meant to stay in orbit for only five years.
"The crew are prepared for all situations. I think they can handle this," he said. "The station can still work as a laboratory."
